## Discussion with the QR-UOV team

As with the other round 3 submission teams throughout September, the first part of the meeting was given over to the QR-UOV team. Rodrigo noted that this was the first time OQS had met with a submission team whose algorithm already has an inclusion PR open in liboqs ([PR #2582](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2582)).

### liboqs integration overview (Bruce)

Bruce presented the integration slides, previously sent to the QR-UOV team:

- **About OQS and liboqs.** liboqs is a curated collection of C implementations of post-quantum algorithms, including the NIST standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) and algorithms standardized elsewhere (e.g. Classic McEliece). In the second half of 2026 the focus has been on signature schemes from the NIST additional signatures on-ramp, now in round 3. Sister projects include oqs-provider (for OpenSSL 3), OpenSSH and BoringSSL integrations, and language wrappers (Python, Rust, Go, and others).
- **Required upstream changes.** NIST submissions share a common API (`crypto_sign_keypair`, `crypto_sign`, `crypto_sign_open`), so implementations must be namespaced to avoid symbol collisions. Implementations should also call liboqs's switchable back-ends for common symmetric primitives (SHA-3/FIPS 202, AES) and randomness in place of their own portable versions.
- **Metadata and automation.** Submitters fill out a YAML metadata file describing parameter sets, build instructions and API names; liboqs's scripts then copy the upstream sources, generate the liboqs API wrappers, CMake files and basic tests (key generation, sign, verify).
- **Tests.** Known-answer tests are hooked in via a SHA-256 checksum of the submission's KAT response file (a quick single-vector check plus a full check of all 100 vectors, run less often). liboqs also runs Valgrind-based constant-time checks, for which contributors must review findings and write suppression files where appropriate, and fuzzing tests.

Bruce invited the team to ping him on the PR or by email with any questions.

### QR-UOV team's plans (Shingo)

Shingo thanked OQS for the invitation and said the process was clear; he expects to have questions once the team begins the work, and will reach out then. He then presented the team's tentative (subject-to-change) schedule:

- **Approval.** The team is currently briefing internal stakeholders. An executive meeting at NTT's lab on **November 2** is expected to give approval for the open-source release of QR-UOV; without it, the team cannot contribute source code.
- **Development.** In parallel, the team is building a development team, including contracting a software development partner. Once contracted, they will refactor the round 3 reference implementation, which Shingo estimates will take about 1–1.5 months. In the best case, the **first PR would come around the beginning of December**, followed by addressing review comments and revising the code into early 2027.

Rodrigo asked what the approval meant, given that the QR-UOV code is already public on GitHub (<https://github.com/qruov/round3>) under a permissive licence, and whether it prevents OQS from incorporating the algorithm. Shingo explained that company rules require executive approval before team members can provide the code to an open-source project. Douglas suggested that the distinction is likely between code being public under a licence, which seems to be the case for QR-UOV, and company employees being able to actively participate in an outside project. He proposed following up by email, and offered to involve Hart.

In answer to Bruce, Shingo said the planned refactoring covers namespacing and API names as described in the presentation. It also covers constant-time behaviour: the current reference implementation is not fully constant-time, and the team will change the code to make it so.

Michael pointed out that there are ongoing discussions about performance and API design on the liboqs PR and, in particular, on a PR directly against the upstream repository ([qruov/round3 PR #1](https://github.com/qruov/round3/pull/1)). He asked whether the team would be open to adapting the implementation's APIs to make integration easier and more performant, since this could feed into their refactoring. Shingo had not been aware of these PRs; he will review them, discuss them with his team, and respond. Rodrigo encouraged the team to comment directly on the PRs so that everyone involved can follow the discussion.

### Status of the QR-UOV inclusion PR

Rodrigo recapped [PR #2582](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2582). Upstream QR-UOV selects one of its 30 variants at compile time via macros, so the first version of the PR duplicated the code for every variant (around 3,000 files). At OQS's request the common code was factored out, bringing the PR down to about 179 files. Work has since been done on splitting the reference and optimized implementations and on the KATs, and partly thanks to Owen's work on making CI more efficient, all tests on the PR now pass.

Paschal introduced himself. He works on post-quantum mitigations for libp2p (a hybrid Noise handshake for the JS, Python and Rust implementations, plus signatures on the discovery side), and got involved with QR-UOV because he needs it for that research. He has tested the PR on his side and contributed CI fixes, including for missing KAT digests, which now pass. The only outstanding item for his part is for Orlando to merge a PR Paschal opened against Orlando's branch. Orlando had audio problems and could not speak, so further discussion with him will continue on GitHub. In the chat, Orlando asked Shingo for contact details for future queries.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Orlando):** Merge Paschal's PR into the QR-UOV inclusion branch.

## liboqs

### Round 3 algorithm inclusion

All four round 3 algorithms being worked on now have PRs open, which Rodrigo described as great progress.

**SDitH ([PR #2586](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2586), Owen).** Two items remain. First, after a chat between Owen, Douglas and Bruce, the AES shimming approach is being revisited. Of the approaches previously posted, the current preference is to add context-release handling within the SDitH repository, since it seems to need the least rework on both the SDitH and liboqs sides; Owen will put this into the PR so it can be evaluated. Second, the Zephyr builds fail because the SDitH implementations use more heap memory than the Zephyr virtual machine allocates. The proposed fix, raised in a comment by Frauschi, is to increase the VM's memory. Rodrigo said a lower-memory upstream implementation would be the better solution. He suggested first confirming that the extra memory comes from the upstream code rather than from the liboqs wrapping, and noted that increasing the memory is probably the quick fix. Douglas had no strong view either way. The CI speed-up merged last week ([PR #2595](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2595)) has helped this and other PRs.

**SQIsign ([PR #2593](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2593), Basil).** All tests pass, including the extended tests. The PR currently imports from a staging repository, which Basil will switch to the official upstream repository before marking it ready. The staging copy contains a few minor changes, notably removing two or three variable-length arrays, which the Windows (MSVC) builds do not support. Basil will ask the SQIsign team to review these changes so they can be merged upstream. The oqs-provider integration can proceed in parallel against the staging branch so it can be tested right away.

**FAEST ([PR #2592](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2592), Norm).** The AES-192 support PR ([PR #2571](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2571)) has been merged, and Norm has opened the draft FAEST integration PR, which he is still working through.
